entry.title: Fixing settings titles at the largest text size
entry.content:
Sarukani's screenshot tour found four settings titles truncated at the largest Dynamic Type size. The rows measured the explanatory text correctly, but the title labels were free to give their parent a one-line ideal height. When the layout came back at that height, longer titles ended in an ellipsis.

The shared SettingLabel now fixes its vertical size while still allowing horizontal wrapping. Three standalone rows use the same rule. I added hosted layout tests for the settings page because they render real SwiftUI views in a window and catch the sizing behavior without paying for a full UI launch on every case.

This fits the verification split I am using in the project. The package suite has 647 tests and runs in about 1.7 seconds. The app unit bundle has 200 tests and takes about 56 seconds because it includes rendered layout cases. The 17 UI tests take about 222 seconds, while the light-and-dark capture tour takes at least four minutes. Captures remain useful, but once one exposes a layout rule, a hosted test is the cheaper regression check.

entry.title: Fixing the sandboxed Core ML path
entry.content:
After I enabled the App Sandbox, KiFinder scans completed with zero detected faces. The progress UI still finished, which made the failure look like a valid album with no matches.

The Core ML setup compiled its model into a hard-coded directory under /private/tmp. A sandboxed app could not write there, the session failed to initialize, and a try? converted that error into nil for every embedding. The fix was to derive the scratch directory from the system temporary directory, which places it inside the app container.

I checked the change with the real engine over saved photos. The broken build produced zero embeddings; the fixed build produced five and six for the same inputs. I also stopped re-scoring the full album after every keep or skip. Re-scoring now runs from an explicit “Find new matches” action and uses one batched matrix multiplication per album.

The missing error handling still needs improvement. A model that cannot initialize should stop the scan and explain the failure instead of returning an empty result that looks successful.

entry.title: Separating generated and author-provided furigana
entry.content:
Aoede's furigana errors came from two different sources, so I built a small harness to separate them before changing the reader. FuriganaQA runs the production pipeline over Aozora books and compares each result with the ruby supplied in the text. A mismatch is either something the generator should have produced or a reading it could not infer.

The first group exposed fixable problems. Aoede was taking phonetic forms from OpenJTalk, so long vowels were written as they sound instead of the expected spelling. It also grouped mixed kanji runs too broadly. Switching to orthographic readings and using JmdictFurigana for per-kanji placement fixed those cases, with JMdict validating the result.

The second group includes readings chosen by an author, such as 本気 read as マジ. No analyzer can recover that choice from the characters. Aoede now preserves ruby from Aozora markup and EPUB <ruby> elements, gives it priority over generated furigana, and uses it for speech as well as display.

The harness made the boundary testable: published ruby wins when it exists, dictionaries handle known readings, and OpenJTalk fills the remaining gaps.

entry.title: Adding the KiFinder review app
entry.content:
KiFinder now has a Mac app around the matching engine. I can enroll a person by dropping in five to twelve reference photos, choose an album or the preschool's zip files, and review the scan without typing photo identifiers into a command.

The review is split into three groups. Confident matches start selected, borderline scores appear under “Worth a look,” and the remaining photos stay out of the main path. Every decision can be changed before saving. In a group photo, the inspector draws a box around each detected face and lets me choose the intended person. That avoids treating the highest-scoring face as the answer when several people are in the photo.

The kept photos go into a library grouped by person and month, ready to export to Photos. The app still writes the same manifest as the command-line engine, so the UI did not need a second data format. It is a view over decisions the engine already records.

For the screenshots I enrolled myself and used synthetic faces for everyone else. That kept the demo useful without putting a preschool album on a public page.

entry.title: Switching Kokoro from Core ML to MLX
entry.content:
Aoede's first Kokoro integration ran through FluidAudio and Core ML. That was the natural on-device path, but it crashed on my M5 Mac with every compute option I tried. The GPU reported a Metal JIT error, while CPU and the Neural Engine failed lower in BNNS. The same library worked on older Apple silicon, so the model itself was probably not the problem.

I replaced that runtime with an MLX port of Kokoro. MLX runs on the M5 and provides a timestamp for each token, which improved the synchronized word highlight at the same time. It does require the Metal toolchain and a real GPU, so the provider belongs in the app target rather than a package built with plain swift build. The iOS Simulator cannot run it and falls back to Apple speech.

I kept the Core ML work on a branch in case its hardware support changes. For now, MLX is the better fit because it works on the machines I use and gives the reader more precise timing.
